newsitem.title: UK: Oil-related FDI is losing importance - UNCTAD.
newsitem.headline: Oil-related FDI is losing importance - UNCTAD.

text.p: Foreign direct investment (FDI) into West Asia is shifting from the oil industry to manufacturing and services, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said on Tuesday.
This mainly reflected decreasing flows to Saudi Arabia, from an average level of $5.0 billion a year during 1982-1985 to $700 million per year during 1990-1995.
"This profound decrease indicates that oil-related FDI is losing importance," UNCTAD added in its latest World Investment report.

Recently FDI into non-oil producing economies (Cyprus, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, areas under the Palestinian Authority, Syrian Arab Republic and Yemen) has been growing faster than that in oil-producing economies (Bahrain, Islamic Republic of Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates), UNCTAD said.

Foreign investors from developed countries have become quite active in the region, with France and the United Kingdom the most active investors. Germany has increased its presence and Japanese investors are being attracted to the regions' petroleum and other natural resources.
A major objective of West Asian countries has recently been to improve their image to non-Arab investors, UNCTAD said.
In the early 1980s, the oil-producing economies dominated investment flows, accounting for over 96 percent of the total inflows to the region.
By the late 1980s, the share of the oil-producing economies had declined substantially to 67 percent.
By the mid-1990s flows to West Asia were almost equally distributed between the groups of oil and non-oil producing countries.
Among the non-oil producing countries, Israel has emerged as a significant FDI recipient, UNCTAD said.
